subject: palm cockatoo
title: This Parrot Makes Its Own Drumsticks and Keeps a Perfect Beat

scenes.text: One bird makes its own drumstick. Then it keeps the beat.
The palm cockatoo, on Australia's Cape York Peninsula. A male fashions a thick stick from a branch, grips it in his foot, and hammers a hollow tree.
Scientists recorded 18 males and 131 drum solos, some 92 taps long. The taps were almost perfectly spaced, like a drummer holding a beat.
Each male has his own signature. Some drum fast, some slow, and they stick to their style.
It's a courtship show. About 70 percent of the drumming happened with a female watching, mixed with calls and a raised crest.
No other animal is known to make a tool just to make music. Only us, and this bird.

description:
Male palm cockatoos make their own drumsticks and tap out a regular beat on hollow trees, the only known case of a non-human animal crafting a tool to make music.
A team led by Robert Heinsohn of the Australian National University recorded 131 drumming sequences from 18 wild males on Cape York Peninsula, Australia, published in Science Advances in 2017. Sequences ran from 5 to 92 taps, spaced almost perfectly evenly, and each male kept a consistent personal style; some were reliably fast, others slow. The drumming is part of a courtship display, about 70 percent of it performed with a female present, combined with calls and a raised crest.
Which animal would you most like to hear jam?
first_comment: 18 males, 131 drum solos, each with his own style. Would a steady beat win you over?
